newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen comes off US highs to end little changed.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen comes off US highs to end little changed.

text.p: *Dlr/yen ends slightly weaker but little changed in US after intra-day surge of near-45 month high of 116.20. *Techs say 115.30 close keeps move intact, next target 117.30. *Weak Nikkei, continued low Japanese rates fuel yen weakness. *Sterling, helped by prospects for UK rate hike, sets fresh intra-day 50-mo high of $1.6945. Stg/yen also near 4-yr highs.
The dollar ended little changed versus the yen on Friday, after an intra-day rally took the greenback to its highest level against the Japanese currency in almost 45 months.
Concerns about a weak Japanese economy and stock market weighed on the yen in thin holiday trading for the second day in a row.

The weak volume, which exaggerated currency fluctuations throughout the week, prompted a series of other major currency moves on Friday, pushing the British pound to a four-year peak against the dollar and nudging the dollar to its highest level against the Swiss franc in almost two-and-a-half years.

"The three trends that have been evident all year long have re-exerted themselves," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole. "We're seeing more weakening of the yen against European currencies and the dollar, a weak Swiss franc, and strong sterling."

The dollar surged as high as 116.20 yen around midday, its highest rate since March 31, 1993, before settling at 115.25/35 against 115.45/55 at the open. The dollar ended modestly weaker at 1.5540/50 marks versus 1.5578/83 in early trade.

Despite a modest rise in the Nikkei index of 225 leading Japanese shares on Friday, the continued frailty of Tokyo's stock market remained a primary focus in the foreign exchange market. The Nikkei average closed at 19,369.04 on Friday, well below the crucial 20,000 threshold.
"It's just a continuation of what we've seen," said John McCarthy, foreign exchange manager at ING Barings Capital Markets Inc, referring to the dollar's intra-day rise against the yen.
"It's a fear of the Nikkei, concerns about the Japanese financial system, low interest rates in Japan and higher interest rates everywhere else in the world," he noted.

A primary beneficiary of broad yen weakness was sterling. Hopes for another rate hike in Britain were fueled earlier in the week when Bank of England Governor Eddie George said that Britain may need to raise interest rates before the next general election to keep its economy from overheating.
The promise of continued low rates in Japan and higher rates in Britain spurred active selling of yen for pounds on Friday, taking the sterling-yen cross rate to its top level in roughly four years.

"Even if British rates stay where they are, relative to what we think will happen in Japan, sterling is still a pretty good value," said Mark Gargano, chief foreign exchange dealer at First Union National Bank.

The pound also surged against the dollar, reaching a peak of $1.6945 in late afternoon trade, its highest threshold since October 1992. Sterling ended the day at $1.6915/25, up from $1.6860/70 at the open and $1.6735/45 on Thursday.
The dollar was a better performer against the Swiss franc, which has been plagued in recent months by the sluggish state of the Swiss economy and low Swiss interest rates.
The dollar held onto overseas gains against the Swiss franc, rising to a fresh 29-month high of 1.3515, before ending the day at 1.3480/90 against 1.3498/08 at the open.
Elsewhere, the dollar ended at Canadian $1.3677/82, up from C$1.3652/57 at the open. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7948/55 against $0.7960/65 at the open.
